newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No pollution threat seen from stricken carrier.
newsitem.headline: No pollution threat seen from stricken carrier.

text.p: There was little threat of an oil spill from a stricken bulk carrier that ran aground about 900 miles (1,440 km) off the west coast of Australia in the Indian Ocean last week, maritime and salvage officials said on Tuesday.

Repair work expected to last 10 days was underway to salvage the 150,000 DWT Goodwill, which on Thursday struck a seamount -- an underwater volcano -- before towing the vessel into deep water to unload its cargo of iron ore, an official of salvager Smit International in Singapore, Edward Teh, told Reuters.
Eventually, the Panamanian-flagged vessel would be dry-docked for more extensive repairs, most likely in Singapore, Teh said.
He said there was only a "remote possibility" that a spill could occur at this stage of the repair work.
The Australian Maritime Rescue Co-Ordination Centre said it was satisified the vessel posed little threat to nearby waters.
"It was fairly well established that there is no imminent danger of pollution, or anything like that," a spokesman for the centre said.

The fully laden vessel was carrying 145,000 tonnes of iron ore from RIO Tinto Ltd/Plc's Hamersley Iron Ore Pty Ltd, 1,130 tonnes of heavy fuel oil and 107 tonnes of diesel when it hit the rocks 60 miles (96 km) southwest of the Cocos Islands while on a trip from Dampier, Western Australia to the Suez Canal.
All 21 crew members were picked up by a British tanker on Friday after abandoning the Korean-owned ship.
